title: General words for change, amount and degree
blurb: Know the HESI A2 words for going up, going down and how much (abate, augment, deplete, negligible, copious) and dodge their look-alikes.
question: A discharge note says the patient's pain should abate, her fluid intake should be augmented and the risk of bleeding is negligible. Which way is each thing moving, and how big is each amount?

teach.body: Formally, these are general academic words that describe the direction of a change (increase or decrease), its speed, and the size of an amount. In plain English: most of them answer one of two questions. Is it going up or down? How much is there? On the HESI A2 they appear in health sentences (a fever abates, a supply is depleted), and the trap is usually the opposite direction or a look-alike word.

head: Word
Part of speech
Meaning
teach.caption: Enhance is about quality (better), not size: enhance safety, enhance flavor.

head: Word
Part of speech
Meaning
teach.caption: Deteriorate (to become worse) is the opposite of ameliorate (to make better).
The HESI A2 often offers the opposite word's meaning as a distractor.

teach.h: How much? Degree words, smallest to largest

items: The nurse expected the fever to subside by morning (become less severe).
A protein shake can supplement small meals (add to them).
Heavy sweating can deplete sodium (use it up).
The scar will be negligible (too small to matter), not invisible.
Profuse bleeding soaked the dressing (flowing in large amounts).
A deficit (noun) is a shortfall: a fluid deficit means too little fluid.

teach.h: Scenario: Aaliyah reads a care note
teach.body: Aaliyah Brooks, applying to an RN program, volunteers at a clinic and reads: 'Swelling has begun to abate; supplies of gauze are depleted; bleeding was negligible; augment fluids.' She sorts each word. Abate: down, so the swelling is easing. Depleted: down to nothing, so gauze must be reordered. Negligible: tiny, not zero. Augment: up, so the patient should drink more. Four words, four directions, no guessing.

teach.text: Degree matters. Negligible is not 'none,' copious is not 'some,' and moderate is not 'mild.' Also watch the topic-fit trap: in 'The swelling began to abate,' an option such as 'was measured' fits the sentence but is not what abate means.

steps.label: Substitute
steps.sub: the option must fit the sentence

items: Up: augment, enhance, escalate, proliferate, supplement, replenish, expedite.
Down: abate, subside, diminish, dwindle, deplete, inhibit, impede.
Amount: negligible < sufficient < moderate < marked/substantial < copious/profuse < excessive.
Look-alikes: abet, negligent, inhabit, replete, supplant, impend.

summary: You can now tell whether a general HESI A2 word describes an increase, a decrease or an amount, and how large that amount is. You can also reject the look-alike and opposite-direction distractors such as abet, negligent, inhabit and replete.

A.q: By evening the swelling in his ankle had begun to subside, so he removed the ice pack. What is the best definition of the word subside in this sentence?
A.why: Subside means to become less intense or severe; he removed the ice because the swelling was going down.

whyNot.0: Spreading describes where swelling goes, a topic fit; subside is about how severe it is.
whyNot.2: This is the opposite of subside.
whyNot.3: A bruise may darken, a topic fit, but subside means to lessen.

A.q: Wearing tinted glasses can diminish the glare that bothers patients after cataract surgery. What is the best definition of the word diminish in this sentence?
A.why: Diminish means to make or become smaller or less; the glasses reduce the glare.

whyNot.0: Destroy is demolish, a look-alike; glasses lessen glare, they do not destroy it.
whyNot.1: Increase (augment) is the opposite of diminish.
whyNot.2: Warn about is admonish, another look-alike.

A.q: Her provider suggested iron tablets to supplement the iron she gets from her diet. What is the best definition of the word supplement in this sentence?
A.why: To supplement is to add something to make up for a lack; the tablets add to dietary iron.

whyNot.0: Replacing is supplant, the look-alike; the tablets add to the diet, they do not take its place.
whyNot.2: Measuring iron is a topic fit (a blood test), but supplement means to add to.
whyNot.3: The body absorbs iron, a topic fit, but supplement describes adding to a supply.

B.q: Loose rugs and clutter can impede a patient's ability to walk safely with a cane. What is the best definition of the word impede in this sentence?
B.why: Impede means to slow or block progress; clutter gets in the way of safe walking.

whyNot.0: Making easier is the opposite (expedite or facilitate).
whyNot.1: Being about to happen is impend, the look-alike.
whyNot.3: Clutter is not needed for walking; impede means to hinder.

B.q: The physical therapist will modify the exercise plan if the patient's knee pain returns next week. What is the best definition of the word modify in this sentence?
B.why: Modify means to change slightly; the therapist will adjust the plan.

whyNot.2: Canceling ends the plan; modify means changing it, not stopping it.

B.q: The patient's profuse sweating soaked the bed sheets within an hour of the fever spiking. What is the best definition of the word profuse in this sentence?
B.why: Profuse means given or flowing in large amounts; soaked sheets show a large amount.

whyNot.1: Slight is the opposite of profuse.
whyNot.2: Widely spread is diffuse, a look-alike; profuse is about quantity.
whyNot.3: Very deep is profound, another look-alike.

C.q: There was a marked improvement in her breathing after the first nebulizer treatment in the clinic. What is the best definition of the word marked in this sentence?
C.why: As an adjective before a noun, marked means clearly noticeable: a marked improvement is an obvious one.

whyNot.0: Barely noticeable is the opposite of marked.
whyNot.2: Written down is the verb sense (to mark); here marked describes the size of the improvement.
whyNot.3: Speed is a topic fit, but marked describes how noticeable the change is, not how fast.

C.q: The new evening clinic hours led to a substantial drop in emergency room visits for minor injuries. What is the best definition of the word substantial in this sentence?
C.why: Substantial means large in amount, size or importance.

whyNot.1: Sudden describes timing; substantial describes size.
whyNot.2: Gradual also describes timing, not size.

C.q: Which word means to become worse?

whyNot.0: Ameliorate means to make better, the opposite.
whyNot.2: Detonate means to explode, a look-alike.
whyNot.3: Deviate means to depart from a usual course, another look-alike.

reteach.title: Think of a volume knob
reteach.question: A music app has a volume knob, a level meter and a mute button. How do those three controls match the words for change, amount and degree?

blocks.h: Turn it up, turn it down, read the meter
blocks.body: Turning the knob up is augment or escalate; turning it down is diminish, abate or subside. Hitting pause on a stalled download is impede; tapping 'boost' is enhance. The level meter shows degree: one bar is negligible, a few bars are moderate, the red zone is excessive. When you meet a change word, ask which control it is: knob up, knob down, or meter reading.

blocks.h: Degree words as a level meter

blocks.text: A knob turned down is not the same as off. Diminished pain is still pain, and a negligible risk is still a risk.

explain.body: Augment (add to), enhance (improve), escalate (intensify), proliferate (multiply), supplement (add to make up a lack), replenish (fill again), expedite (speed up).

test.q: Weeds proliferate quickly in the community garden after a warm spring rain. What is the best definition of the word proliferate in this sentence?
test.why: Proliferate means to increase rapidly in number.

whyNot.0: Wilting is the opposite of thriving.
whyNot.1: Growing taller is a change in size; proliferate is a change in number.
whyNot.3: Color change is a topic fit for plants, but proliferate means to multiply.

explain.body: Abate and subside (become less intense), diminish (become smaller), dwindle (shrink little by little), deplete (use up), inhibit (hold back), impede (block).

test.q: As flu season ended, the number of patients in the clinic's waiting room began to dwindle. What is the best definition of the word dwindle in this sentence?
test.why: Dwindle means to become gradually smaller.

whyNot.0: Rising sharply is the opposite of dwindle.
whyNot.1: Staying the same is no change; dwindle means a gradual decrease.
whyNot.3: Impatience is a topic fit for a waiting room, but dwindle describes number.

explain.body: From least to most: negligible, sufficient, moderate, marked or substantial, copious or profuse, excessive. Excessive means more than is necessary or healthy.

test.q: Excessive use of decongestant nasal spray can make nasal congestion worse over time. What is the best definition of the word excessive in this sentence?
test.why: Excessive means more than is necessary or normal.

whyNot.1: Use as directed is the safe amount; excessive means beyond it.
whyNot.3: Expensive is a sound-alike in rhythm, but excessive is about amount, not cost.

explain.body: negligible (tiny) vs negligent (careless); abate (lessen) vs abet (help a wrongdoer); inhibit (hold back) vs inhabit (live in); deplete (use up) vs replete (full).

test.q: Which word means so small as to be unimportant?
test.why: Negligible means so small or trivial that it can be disregarded.

whyNot.0: Negligent means careless, the classic look-alike.
whyNot.1: Eligible means qualified to be chosen.
whyNot.3: Legible means clear enough to read.
